subject: physics
title: Charging and discharging capacitors
key_idea: A capacitor charges and discharges through a resistor exponentially, not at a steady rate. The time constant τ = RC says how fast. After one time constant a discharging capacitor has fallen to about 37% of its starting value.

sections.heading: Charge flow when charging and discharging

blocks.text: A capacitor charges and discharges through a circuit by electrons flowing in the wires. No electrons cross the insulator between the plates.

items.text: Electrons flow from the negative terminal of the supply onto the plate joined to it. That plate becomes negative.
The same number of electrons leave the other plate and flow to the positive terminal. That plate becomes positive.
As charge builds up, the p.d. across the capacitor opposes the supply. The current falls to zero when the two are equal.
With the supply removed, electrons flow from the negative plate round the circuit, through the resistor, to the positive plate.
The current is in the opposite direction to charging. It falls as the p.d. across the capacitor falls.
The flow stops when both plates are neutral and the p.d. is zero.

items: Charging and discharging are flows of electrons through the circuit, not across the gap.
The current is largest at the start and falls to zero.

blocks.text: A resistor limits the current, so the capacitor charges and discharges gradually. The graphs are exponential curves.

rows: Falls from I₀ to 0, in the opposite direction

diagram.alt: Two exponential curves against time in units of RC. Charging: charge or p.d. across the capacitor rises from zero and levels off at its final value. Discharging: charge, p.d. or current falls from its starting value towards zero.

y.label: Fraction of final or starting value

series.name: Charging (Q or V across the capacitor)

items: The gradient of a Q–t graph is the current, I = ΔQ/Δt. It is steepest at the start.
The area under an I–t graph is the charge that has flowed.
The curves never quite reach their final value: they approach it.
Charge and p.d. rise (charging) or fall (discharging) exponentially.
Current falls exponentially in both cases.
Gradient of Q–t is current. Area under I–t is charge.

blocks.text: The time constant says how quickly the capacitor charges or discharges. It depends on the resistor and the capacitor.

items.meaning: The product of the resistance and the capacitance in the circuit. It is measured in seconds.

items: When discharging, τ is the time for Q, V or I to fall to 1/e of its starting value, about 37%.
When charging, τ is the time for Q or V to rise to about 63% of its final value.
A larger R or a larger C makes τ longer, so charging and discharging take longer.
τ = RC, in seconds.
After one time constant a discharging capacitor has 37% of its initial charge left.

blocks.text: The curves follow exponential equations. The letter e is the base of natural logarithms, 2.718…

blocks.label: Discharging
where: x = Q, V or I at time t

blocks.label: Charging charge or p.d.
where: x = Q or V at time t
x₀ = final value of Q or V

items: When charging, the current still decays: I = I₀ e^(−t/RC), where I₀ = V₀/R.
The p.d. across the resistor follows the same decay as the current, because V = IR.

blocks.text: Where the V and I equations come from

items.text: Q = Q₀ e^(−t/RC) for a discharging capacitor.
Since V = Q/C, V = V₀ e^(−t/RC).
Current is the rate at which charge flows, so I = −ΔQ/Δt. The gradient of Q = Q₀ e^(−t/RC) gives I = I₀ e^(−t/RC), with I₀ = Q₀/RC = V₀/R.

blocks.label: Logarithmic form
blocks.formula: ln x = ln x₀ − t / RC

items: Plot ln x against t. The graph is a straight line.
The gradient is −1/RC, so RC = −1 ÷ gradient.
The intercept on the ln x axis is ln x₀.

diagram.alt: A slider activity. Change the resistance, the capacitance and the time and see the time constant and how far a capacitor has charged or discharged.

inputs.label: Time after the switch is closed

items: Discharge: x = x₀e^(−t/RC). Charge: x = x₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)).
Taking logs gives ln x = ln x₀ − t/RC, a straight line with gradient −1/RC.

blocks.text: Every exponential decay has the same shape. In equal time intervals the quantity falls by the same fraction.

items: After each time T½ the quantity halves. After each time RC it is multiplied by 1/e, about 0.37.
This is the constant-ratio property of an exponential decay graph.

items.text: ½ = e^(−T½/RC).
ln 2 = T½ / RC.
T½ = RC ln 2 = 0.69 RC.

blocks.label: Time to halve
where: T½ = time for Q, V or I to halve (s)

items: Measure the time for a value on the graph to halve, then divide by 0.69 to find RC.
The same T½ is found whichever starting point on the curve you choose.
Equal times give equal fractions.
T½ = 0.69RC.

blocks.text: The investigation measures how the p.d. across a capacitor changes with time while it discharges through a resistor.

items.text: Join a capacitor, a resistor and a switch to a d.c. supply. Put a voltmeter across the capacitor. An ammeter in series measures the current.
Charge the capacitor fully.
Switch to discharge through the resistor and record the p.d. at regular times.
Plot V against t and ln V against t. Find RC from the gradient of the straight line, −1/RC.
Check the result against the value of R × C. Repeat with different R or C.

items: A data logger takes many readings a second, which suits small time constants.
An oscilloscope or data logger shows the whole curve on a screen.
With meters and a stopwatch, use a large R and C so that RC is several seconds.
An electrolytic capacitor is polarised: connect it the correct way round.
Record p.d. at regular times and plot ln V against t.
The gradient of the straight line is −1/RC.

checks.q: A 220 μF capacitor discharges through a 47 kΩ resistor. Calculate the time constant.
A capacitor charged to 6.0 V discharges through a resistor with a time constant of 8.0 s. Calculate the p.d. after 12 s.
Describe how a graph of ln V against t is used to find the time constant of a discharging capacitor.
checks.a: Plot ln V against t. It is a straight line with a negative gradient. The gradient equals −1/RC, so RC = −1 ÷ gradient.

blocks.text: Modelling a discharge step by step
The change in charge in a short time Δt is found from the current at that moment.

items.text: I = V/R and V = Q/C, so I = Q/(CR).
The charge falls as it flows away: ΔQ/Δt = −Q/(CR).
Set Q₀, R, C and a small time step Δt in a spreadsheet.
ΔQ = −Q ÷ (CR) × Δt. The new Q is the old Q plus ΔQ. Fill down.
Graph Q against t. A smaller Δt gives a curve closer to the exponential.

items: On a graph of Q against t, the gradient of the tangent at any point is −Q/(CR).
The same spreadsheet idea works for a charging capacitor.
The equation ΔQ/Δt = −Q/(CR) says the rate of discharge is proportional to the charge left.
This is why the decay is exponential.
